title: Table salt is made of a metal that explodes in water and a poisonous green gas

cover.alt: A tall glass cylinder of pale yellow-green chlorine gas on a lab bench, with a bright orange glow at the bottom where a piece of sodium is burning.

body: [Sodium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium) is a soft metal so reactive that it can explode on contact with water. [Chlorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine) is a yellow-green gas so toxic it was used as a weapon in the First World War. Bring them together and each sodium atom hands one electron to a chlorine atom, the oppositely charged ions lock together into a crystal, and a lot of heat comes out. What is left is **sodium chloride**, ordinary table salt, made of stable ions that no longer react the way the two elements did.

slides.alt: A hand drops a small piece of sodium into a tall cylinder of pale green chlorine gas. The sodium flares bright orange for a few seconds, and the cylinder is left cloudy.
slides.caption: A small piece of sodium goes into a cylinder of pale green chlorine gas. It flares bright orange as the two react, and the cylinder turns cloudy.

left.label: Sodium + chlorine
left.text: A metal soft enough to cut with a knife that reacts violently with water, and a poisonous yellow-green gas.

right.label: Sodium chloride
right.text: Stable white crystals that melt only at 801 °C and that we sprinkle on our food.

slides.heading: From two dangerous elements to salt

steps.label: Each sodium atom gives up one electron
The ions stack into salt crystals

slides.prompt: In a crystal of table salt, how many chloride ions surround each sodium ion?
slides.detail: They sit above, below, left, right, in front and behind, all at right angles. Each chloride ion is surrounded by six sodium ions in the same way.

slides.label: of heat given off for every gram of salt made from sodium and chlorine
slides.text: That is 411 kJ for each mole, or 58.4 g, of sodium chloride.

slides.question: How are sodium metal and chlorine gas mostly made today?
slides.explanation: Electrolysis runs the reaction backwards: sodium comes from molten sodium chloride, and chlorine mostly from salty water, or brine.
